title: How to Use a Spurtle for Sourdough Discard Waffles
meta_description: Learn how to use a spurtle for mixing sourdough discard waffles – step‑by‑step tips, tools, and a skinny wooden spurtle that makes perfect batter every time.
html:
When you’re mixing sourdough discard waffles, the right tool can make the difference between a smooth batter and a lumpy mess. A spurtle – a slender, wooden whisk‑like stick – is perfect for this job. Its narrow profile slides easily into the corners of a jar, scrapes down the sides, and creates a uniform mixture without over‑working the gluten. Below is a practical guide that shows you how to get the most out of a spurtle when turning that sourdough discard into golden, crispy waffles.

Why a Spurtle Beats a Traditional Whisk for Sourdough Discard

A standard balloon whisk is great for aerating batters, but it can also incorporate too much air into a sourdough‑based waffle mix, leading to a fragile crumb. The spurtle’s flat, tapered shape gently folds the discard into the wet ingredients, preserving the natural texture of the starter while still breaking up clumps. Its wooden surface is non‑scratch, so you can use it directly in metal or glass bowls without worrying about damage.

Essential Ingredients & Tools

Before you start mixing, gather these items:

  • 1 cup sourdough discard (fresh or refrigerated)
  • 1 cup all‑purpose flour
  • 1 cup milk (or plant‑based alternative)
  • 2 eggs, lightly beaten
  • 2 tbsp melted butter or oil
  • 1 tbsp sugar
  • 1 tsp baking powder
  • Pinch of salt
  • Wooden Spurtle & Sourdough Starter Stirrer Set (2 pcs)
  • Mixing bowl (medium‑sized)
  • Waffle iron, pre‑heated

The featured 2 pcs wooden spurtle spatula is ideal because the skinny dough stirring stick reaches into the bottom of the jar to scrape every last bit of discard, while the Danish‑style dough whisk gives you extra leverage when folding in the dry ingredients.

Step‑by‑Step: Mixing Sourdough Discard Waffles

  1. Combine wet ingredients. In the mixing bowl, whisk together the sourdough discard, milk, eggs, melted butter, and sugar until the mixture is uniform.
  2. Scrape the jar. Use the wooden spurtle from the set to stir the wet mixture for 30‑45 seconds. The spurtle’s slender tip will pull any stubborn bits of starter from the sides and bottom of the container, ensuring they’re fully incorporated.
  3. Add dry components. Sprinkle the flour, baking powder, and salt over the wet mixture. Using the Danish dough stick, gently fold the dry ingredients into the batter. Avoid vigorous beating; the goal is a smooth batter with a few small lumps.
  4. Rest the batter. Let the mixture sit for 5‑10 minutes. This short rest allows the baking powder to activate and the gluten to relax, giving you a tender interior and crisp exterior.
  5. Cook the waffles. Lightly oil the pre‑heated waffle iron, pour the batter, and close the lid. Cook until the waffles are deep golden and release easily – usually 4‑5 minutes depending on your iron.

Throughout the process, the spurtle’s non‑scratch wooden surface prevents any metal marks on your mixing bowl, and its ergonomic shape reduces hand fatigue during the quick stirring motions.

Tips for Perfect Waffle Texture

Even with the right tool, a few technique tweaks can elevate your waffles:

  • Don’t over‑mix. Over‑mixing develops gluten, resulting in tough waffles. The spurtle’s gentle folding action helps you stop at the right point.
  • Adjust batter thickness. If the batter feels too thick, add a splash of milk; if it’s too runny, sprinkle in a little extra flour. The skinny spurtle makes these adjustments quick and precise.
  • Season creatively. Add a pinch of cinnamon, vanilla extract, or finely chopped herbs for a flavor twist. The spurtle can easily blend in small additions without breaking the batter’s structure.

Cleaning and Caring for Your Wooden Spurtle

After you’ve finished mixing, rinse the spurtle under warm water and wipe it dry with a clean towel. Because it’s wood, avoid soaking it for long periods; instead, lightly oil the handle with food‑grade mineral oil once a month to maintain its durability and prevent cracking. This simple care routine will keep your spurtle ready for the next batch of sourdough discard waffles or any other dough‑mixing task.

FAQ

Can I use the spurtle with a silicone or non‑stick bowl?

Absolutely. The wooden surface is gentle on all bowl types, so you won’t risk scratching a silicone or non‑stick interior.

Is the spurtle suitable for gluten‑free waffle batters?

Yes. Its narrow shape works well with any batter, including gluten‑free mixes. Just give it a quick rinse between uses to avoid cross‑contamination.

How many times can I reuse the same spurtle?

With proper cleaning and occasional oiling, a wooden spurtle can last for years. It’s built to endure daily mixing, scraping, and stirring without losing its shape.
